title: The Prisoner's Dilemma
philosophicalAnchor: The dilemma has no right answer—that is what makes it a dilemma. But computation gives us tools to reason rigorously about it, to see why the paradox is hard and how it illuminates strategic interaction.
pythonConcept: game theory, payoff matrix, Nash equilibrium, strategy pattern, simulation, nested dictionaries
briefDescription: Explore the classic Prisoner's Dilemma through computational modeling, implementing multiple strategies and discovering Nash equilibria.
theoryPillar: The Prisoner's Dilemma: both players defecting (D,D) is the Nash equilibrium—no player can improve by unilaterally changing strategy. Yet (C,C) gives both a better payoff, making it Pareto superior but unstable.
anchorPillar: The trading floor: Cooperate (C) accepts modest fair profit, Defect (D) attempts larger profit at other's expense. Payoff matrix: (C,C)=3,3; (C,D)=0,5; (D,C)=5,0; (D,D)=1,1.
triggerPillar: Four opponent types: Always-Cooperator, Always-Defector, Randomist, Tit-for-Tatter. Against Always-Defector, your best response is to defect even though both cooperating would be better—a paradox of individual vs collective rationality.
realityPillar: Payoff matrix as nested dict: payoff_matrix[(C,D)][you]. Strategy functions take history and return C or D. Tit-for-Tat cooperates first, then mirrors opponent's last move. 100-round simulation loops accumulate payoffs.
